questions.problem:
Let $F(x)={x}^{2}+3$ for $x\in R,$ and let $f(x)$ be the $2\pi $-periodic extension of $F$ from $x\in [-\pi ,\pi )$ to $x\in R.$ The Fourier series of $f$ is given by

$$
f(x)∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)).
$$

Select the correct options in the expression for the coefficient ${a}_{3}$ below, where $⟨\,,⟩$ denotes the usual inner product on functions over $[-\pi ,\pi ).$

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{3} & ={{field-1}} \\  & ={{field-2}}\,\cdot \,{{field-3}}\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
The usual inner product of functions $f$ and $g$ over $x\in [-\pi ,\pi )$ is given by

$$
⟨f(x),g(x)⟩={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f(x)g(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

For a $2\pi $-periodic function $f(x)$ that is piecewise continuous over $x\in [-\pi ,\pi ),$ the Fourier series of $f$ is given by 

$$
f(x)∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)),
$$

where ${a}_{0},$ ${a}_{n},$ and ${b}_{n}$ are constants to be determined. 

Now, we find the inner product of $f(x)$ with $\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x):$

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨f(x),\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)⟩ & = \\ ⟨\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)),\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)⟩ & = \\ ⟨\frac{{a}_{0}}{2},\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)⟩+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }⟨{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx),\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)⟩+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }⟨{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx),\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)⟩ & = \\ \frac{{a}_{0}}{2}⟨1,\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)⟩+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx),\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)⟩+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx),\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Since the functions
$1,\operatorname{sin}⁡(x),\operatorname{cos}⁡(x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x),\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x),…$
are orthogonal with respect to the defined inner product, the only nonzero term in the final expression above is

$$
{a}_{3}⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x),\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)⟩.
$$

Computing the inner product, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x),\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)⟩ & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }{cos}^{2}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{1}{2}x+\frac{1}{12}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6x)]}_{-\pi }^{\pi } \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\pi -(-\pi ))+\frac{1}{12}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(6\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(-6\pi )) \\  & =\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain that

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨f(x),\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)⟩ & ={a}_{3}⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x),\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)⟩ \\ {a}_{3} & =\frac{⟨f(x),\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)⟩}{⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x),\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)⟩} \\ {a}_{3} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }\cdot {\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }({x}^{2}+3)\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Checking Orthogonality of Sines and Cosines
questions.problem:
$$
⟨f(x),g(x)⟩={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }f(x)g(x)\,\text{d}x
$$

Given the inner product on the set of continuous functions over $x\in [0,2\pi )$ defined above, select the correct options below.$\,$
$⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(6x),\operatorname{cos}⁡(6x)⟩=$
{{field-1}}

$\,$
The functions $f(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(6x)$ and $g(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(6x)$ 
{{field-2}}.
questions.worked_solution:
We begin by using the half-angle identity

$$
{cos}^{2}⁡(6x)=\frac{1}{2}(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(12x)).
$$

Substituting this into the integral gives

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(6x),\operatorname{cos}⁡(6x)⟩ & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{cos}^{2}⁡(6x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(12x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{1}{2}x+\frac{1}{24}\operatorname{sin}⁡(12x)]}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(2\pi -0)+\frac{1}{24}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(24\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)) \\  & =\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $f(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(6x)$ and $g(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(6x)$ $\text{are not orthogonal}$ with respect to the inner product.

questions.problem:
$$
⟨f(x),g(x)⟩={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }f(x)g(x)\,\text{d}x
$$

Given the inner product on the set of continuous functions over $x\in [0,2\pi )$ defined above, select the correct options below.$\,$
$⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x),\operatorname{cos}⁡(7x)⟩=$
{{field-1}}

$\,$
The functions $f(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)$ and $g(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(7x)$ 
{{field-2}}.
questions.worked_solution:
We begin by using the product-to-sum identity

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(7x)=\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(9x)).
$$

Substituting this into the integral gives

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x),\operatorname{cos}⁡(7x)⟩ & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(7x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(9x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{1}{10}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x)+\frac{1}{18}\operatorname{sin}⁡(9x)]}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{1}{10}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(10\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0))+\frac{1}{18}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(18\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)) \\  & =\frac{1}{10}(0-0)+\frac{1}{18}(0-0) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $f(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)$ and $g(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(7x)$ $\text{are orthogonal}$ with respect to the inner product.

questions.problem:
Let $F(x)=3x+1$ for $x\in R,$ and let $f(x)$ be the $2\pi $-periodic extension of $F$ from $x\in [0,2\pi )$ to $x\in R.$ The Fourier series of $f$ is given by

$$
f(x)∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)).
$$

Select the correct options in the expression for the coefficient ${a}_{0}$ below, where $⟨\,,⟩$ denotes the usual inner product on functions over $[0,2\pi ).$

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{0} & ={{field-1}} \\  & ={{field-2}}\,\cdot \,{{field-3}}\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
The usual inner product of functions $f$ and $g$ over $x\in [0,2\pi )$ is given by

$$
⟨f(x),g(x)⟩={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }f(x)g(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

For a $2\pi $-periodic function $f(x)$ that's piecewise continuous over $x\in [0,2\pi ),$ the Fourier series of $f$ is given by 

$$
f(x)∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)),
$$

where ${a}_{0},$ ${a}_{n},$ and ${b}_{n}$ are constants to be determined. 

Now, we find the inner product of $f(x)$ with $1:$

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨f(x),1⟩ & = \\ ⟨\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)),1⟩ & = \\ ⟨\frac{{a}_{0}}{2},1⟩+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }⟨{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx),1⟩+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }⟨{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx),1⟩ & = \\ \frac{{a}_{0}}{2}⟨1,1⟩+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx),1⟩+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx),1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Since the functions
$1,\operatorname{sin}⁡(x),\operatorname{cos}⁡(x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x),\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x),…$
are orthogonal with respect to the defined inner product, the only nonzero term in the final expression above is

$$
\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}⟨1,1⟩.
$$

Computing the inner product, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨1,1⟩ & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }1\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[x]}_{-0}^{2\pi } \\  & =2\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain that

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨f(x),1⟩ & =\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}⟨1,1⟩ \\ {a}_{0} & =\frac{2⟨f(x),1⟩}{⟨1,1⟩} \\ {a}_{0} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }\cdot {\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(3x+1)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the inner product, we have
